problem.text:
Alice and Bob play a game on a sphere which is initially marked with a finite number of points. Alice and Bob then take turns making moves, with Alice going first:
- On Alice's move, she counts the number of marked points on the sphere, n. She then marks another n+1 points on the sphere.
- On Bob's move, he chooses one hemisphere and removes all marked points on that hemisphere, including any marked points on the boundary of the hemisphere.
Can Bob always guarantee that after a finite number of moves, the sphere contains no marked points?
(A hemisphere is the region on a sphere that lies completely on one side of any plane passing through the centre of the sphere.)

goal.asked: Whether Bob has a strategy that empties the sphere against every possible play by Alice.
goal.answer_form: Yes or no, with proof. If yes: a strategy for Bob plus a proof that it terminates. If no: a strategy for Alice that keeps at least one point forever.
goal.final_line_would_say: After every round the number of marked points strictly decreases, so after finitely many rounds it is zero.

informal_cues.bearing: Alice moves first, so each round is add-then-remove. The quantity to control is the count left after Bob.
'Always' means Bob cannot rely on Alice placing points badly; the strategy must beat the worst case.
'Finite' at the start means the count is a natural number from the first move, so induction and descent are available.

underneath.really_is: a closed surface with central symmetry and no boundary
underneath.implies: every great circle passes through antipodal pairs; there is no edge for points to hide at

underneath.really_is: the intersection of the sphere with a closed half-space whose boundary plane contains the centre
underneath.implies: its boundary is a great circle, and because the region is closed, points on that circle are removed

underneath.really_is: choosing a plane through the centre, then a side
underneath.implies: for any plane the two closed hemispheres cover every point, so one side contains at least half of them

deeper_properties: Through the centre and any two points on the sphere there is a plane, so Bob can always place two marked points on the boundary.
Count argument: if $m$ points remain and the plane passes through two of them, one closed hemisphere contains at least $2 + \lceil (m-2)/2 \rceil = \lceil (m+2)/2 \rceil > m/2$ points.
'At least half' only stops growth; 'more than half' forces decrease. The boundary clause is what upgrades one to the other.

simplification.instance: Play the same game on a circle. Alice adds n+1 points; Bob removes a closed semicircle (a diameter through the centre and one side).
simplification.instance_latex: \text{Start with one point. Alice adds } 2 \text{, giving } 3 \text{ points. Can Bob remove all } 3 \text{?}
simplification.what_to_try: Place the three points $120^\circ$ apart. Check whether any closed semicircle contains all three. Then ask how many marked points a diameter can pass through.
simplification.notice_prompt: In two dimensions a diameter passes through one marked point and its antipode at most, and Bob cannot clear three spread-out points. On a sphere, how many marked points can a plane through the centre pass through, and what does the boundary clause let Bob do with that?

candidates.name: Monovariant: show the count strictly decreases every round
candidates.from_first_principles: The goal is termination, and termination arguments need a quantity in the natural numbers that strictly decreases. The count after Bob's move is the obvious quantity. Alice takes it from $n$ to $2n+1$, so Bob must remove at least $n+2$ to leave at most $n-1$. Putting the plane through two marked points guarantees removing $\lceil (2n+3)/2 \rceil = n+2$.
candidates.why: It answers the exact question asked and every step is forced by a span.

candidates.name: Induction on the number of points
candidates.from_first_principles: Finite initial count suggests induction on $n$.
candidates.why: It is the same argument as the monovariant in different clothing; the monovariant is cleaner to state.

candidates.name: Find an Alice strategy that keeps points forever
candidates.from_first_principles: If the answer were no, we would need a configuration Bob cannot shrink. Spreading points evenly is the natural try.
candidates.why: Any configuration is beaten by a plane through two of its points, so no such strategy exists.

candidates.name: Potential function on positions of points
candidates.from_first_principles: Geometric spread of points could be measured.
candidates.why: Far heavier than needed; the count alone suffices.

method.chosen: Monovariant with the two-point plane lemma: after each round at most $n-1$ points remain, so Bob wins.
